newsitem.title: USA: Airline stocks jump on strong first quarter view.
newsitem.headline: Airline stocks jump on strong first quarter view.

text.p: Shares of U.S. airlines jumped Tuesday after UAL Corp forecast that first quarter earnings would exceed Wall Street estimates.
The bullish forecast from UAL, the parent company of United Airlines, set an upbeat tone for the rest of the sector, analysts said.

Carriers have benefitted from the lapse of the passenger excise tax and labor disruption at AMR Corp's American Airlines, analysts said. First quarter revenues and load factors will likely be stronger than year-ago results.
UAL said it expects first quarter earnings to exceed the highest analyst estimate on First Call of $1.30 per fully distributed share. A year earlier the airline earned $0.77 a share.
UAL gained three points to 62-7/8 in early training. Delta Air Lines Inc was up 1-5/8 at 83-7/8, AMR Corp gained 1-1/4 to 82, and Continental Airlines Inc increased 3/4 to 29-3/4.
The Dow Jones transport index was up more than 27 points to 2400.
The threat of a strike by American Air pilots created a first quarter windfall for rival carriers, especially United. Passengers shied away from American as the February 15 strike deadline loomed.

"Some airlines benefitted from the disruptions at American. United and American share a hub in Chicago, so United got a boost for about a week to 10 days," said Jeffrey Long, an analyst with J.P. Morgan.
Continental and Delta also absorbed additional travelers and "good will" during American's labor problems, analysts said.
President Clinton imposed a cooling-off period on American and its pilots, preventing a strike, and travelers were later wooed back to the carrier by deep fare discounts.
Airlines also benefitted in the first quarter from the lapsed passenger excise tax.
"The airlines are getting a better boost from the excise tax this year," said Brian Harris, a analyst with Lehman Brothers.
Airlines have culled extra revenues since January 1 by pocketing the 10 percent tax that would normally go the the federal government. The tax is expected to be reinstated within the next two weeks.
The tax was absent last year as well. Airlines initially passed on the savings to consumers, but then slowly raised fares throughout the year.
This year, airlines are keeping the extra money for themselves.
Carriers may try to raise fares when the tax is reinstated. If consumers balk, carriers may have to increase fares more slowly, analysts said.
